answer.label: Not verified as Nietzsche’s words — a modern paraphrase
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment — that people prefer comforting belief to hard inquiry — is genuinely Nietzschean, but this exact aphorism appears in none of his books, letters or notebooks and is listed under the Misattributed section of Wikiquote with no source. Its nearest authentic ancestor is his 1865 letter to his sister Elisabeth: “if you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.”

source.excerpt: Most people are not seeking truth; they are searching for comfort in illusions.
trail: The exact line is catalogued under “Misattributed” on Wikiquote’s Nietzsche page, with no work or citation attached.
No book, essay, letter or notebook of Nietzsche’s is known to contain this wording; it reads as a 21st-century motivational paraphrase rather than his prose.
The genuine idea traces to his 1865 letter to his devout sister Elisabeth: believe for peace of soul, or inquire to be a devotee of truth.
source.excerptNote: This is the circulating internet wording. It matches no passage in Nietzsche’s corpus; the closest thing he actually wrote is the 1865 letter quoted below.
source.rightsNote: The circulating wording has no identifiable author or first-publication date — it appears to be an anonymous modern paraphrase, so no copyright status can be asserted. (Nietzsche’s own 1865 letter is long in the public domain, but that is a different text.)

author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher whose work on morality, truth and self-deception — from Human, All Too Human to Beyond Good and Evil — reshaped modern thought. He wrote often about how people cling to comforting beliefs, which is exactly why sleek modern aphorisms in that vein get pinned on him. His actual prose is denser and more qualified than the one-line versions that circulate online.

misattribution.heading: How this got pinned on Nietzsche
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook feel-good misattribution: a polished modern one-liner draped over a famous philosopher whose real writing happens to touch the same theme.

items.why: The sentence appears in no Nietzsche book, essay, letter or notebook. It is catalogued under “Misattributed” on Wikiquote and circulates only in recent motivational posts and videos.
The belief-versus-inquiry contrast is authentically his, expressed in the 1865 letter to Elisabeth — but in different words.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the thought is broadly Nietzschean, but the sentence is not his — it’s an unsourced modern paraphrase that Wikiquote lists as misattributed.

context.heading: Why the real version is sharper
lead: Nietzsche’s actual formulation, written at twenty to his religious sister, frames it as a fork in the road: “if you wish to strive for peace of soul and pleasure, then believe; if you wish to be a devotee of truth, then inquire.” It offers a choice rather than an accusation.
The viral rewrite flattens that into a verdict about “most people” — punchier for social media, but not something Nietzsche ever wrote.
context.pull: Believe for peace of soul, or inquire to be a devotee of truth — Nietzsche’s real 1865 words.
